root.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Exchange Variation
root.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 d5 4. cxd5

sources.title: Search snippets: QGD Exchange, Carlsbad structure and kingside e4 plan (kingsights.net, thechessworld.com, houseofstaunton.com)

overview: White exchanges on d5 at once, giving the Carlsbad pawn structure after ...exd5: White has a central d4 pawn and a queenside majority-in-reverse, Black has c6/d5. White's signature plan is the queenside minority attack (a4, b4-b5) to fix a backward c6 pawn; the alternative is to hold the centre and push e2-e4 for a kingside attack. Black counters with ...c5, the ...f5 break or an e-file/kingside push, and aims to use the knight outpost on c4. The 5.Bg5 Positional Variation (5.Bg5 Be7/c6) is the most common branch; Black can also recapture 4...Nxd5 with a different structure. The game is slow and plan-based, with the pawn structure telling both sides where to play. Almost every world champion has played both sides, and the theory is well mapped.

white_ideas.idea: Minority attack: bring the b- and a-pawns forward (a4, b4, b5) to provoke ...cxb5 or a backward pawn on c6, then target it with rooks on the c-file.
Alternatively hold the centre and push e2-e4 at the right moment for a kingside or central attack, usually with Bd3, Nge2/Nf3 and Qc2.
5.Bg5 (Positional Variation) pins the f6 knight so White controls e5 and pressures d5 before choosing a plan.
Convert structural advantages into a favourable endgame with a passed pawn after the queenside is opened.

black_ideas.idea: Defend d5 and control e4 with a solid set-up (...Be7, ...O-O, ...c6, ...Nbd7), keeping the position compact.
Counter in the centre with ...c5, with the ...f5 break, or with e4/e5 pushes and kingside attack while White spends time on the minority attack.
Use the knight outpost on c4 (the 'useful square' for a knight) after White's pawns advance.

typical_structures.structure: Carlsbad: White c-pawn gone, d4 pawn against Black c6/d5 (Black e-pawn gone to d5): White's two queenside pawns (a, b) face Black's three (a, b, c). Minority attack target is c6.
After 4...Nxd5 the structure is different: Black has d5 gone and e4 and c-pawn options; more open and more dynamic centre.

character.notes: Chessiverse: 'strategically rich' with emphasis on long-term plans over tactics. Plans are slow: a minority attack takes many moves, giving Black time for counterplay. One snippet source says it is 'anything but quiet' despite the name. Not forcing; but when White goes for the e4 kingside plan and Black for ...f5 the game can turn sharp.

gambit.notes: The name 'Gambit' is historical; White simply exchanges pawns on d5.

soundness.notes: Sound for both sides. Chessiverse: structure sound but demands deep understanding; almost every world champion has played both sides. Win rates over 36.7 million games are White 50.9 percent, Black 44 percent, draws 5.1 percent, with draws rising to 10.9 percent at 2500 Elo.

structure.notes: The central d4 and d5 pawns face each other with the c-file semi-open for White after cxd5 exd5; the centre is fixed and tense rather than open. Play happens on the wings: minority attack on the queenside, kingside/central breaks for Black. Mostly closed centre where manoeuvring comes before contact.

approach.notes: A mainline opening, not a system: it follows from the QGD move order. Played by Alekhine (113 games as White), Marshall (109) and Klovans (121 as Black) in the data; strong players still choose it (almost every world champion has played both sides).

level.notes: Chessiverse labels it Advanced/Theoretician but the emphasis is on plans: the structure is sound but demands deep understanding. The Carlsbad plans (minority attack, e4 break, ...c5/...f5 counters) are well documented and learnable; the memory load is moderate because the main lines are not forcing. For club players the plans are comprehensible but need study to execute.

sublines_that_differ.name: 4...Nxd5
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 Nxd5
sublines_that_differ.how: Black avoids the Carlsbad and plays for a freer, more open centre, with e4 in mind; a different structure and character from the mainline.

sublines_that_differ.name: Positional Variation 5.Bg5
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 Nf6 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 d5 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Bg5
sublines_that_differ.how: Most common branch; White pins the knight. Black's ...Be7 or ...c6 decide the structure.

sublines_that_differ.name: 5.Nf3 lines
sublines_that_differ.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 e6 3. Nc3 Nf6 4. cxd5 exd5 5. Nf3 c6
sublines_that_differ.how: Quieter development with Nf3 and Bf4/Bg5 later; similar Carlsbad play.

description.claim: The Exchange Variation immediately clarifies the central pawn structure, leading to a strategically rich and often symmetrical game.
description.note: Chessiverse: strategically rich. After exd5 the structure is semi-symmetrical (the Carlsbad), asymmetrical on the queenside.

description.claim: White's primary plan is the 'minority attack' on the queenside (b4-b5), aiming to create a weakness in Black's camp.
description.note: Alternative plan is e2-e4 and a kingside attack, so the minority attack is a main rather than the only plan.

description.claim: It is a strategic, plan-based opening rather than a sharp, tactical one.
description.note: Chessiverse emphasises long-term positional plans over tactics.

common_plans.claim: White executes the minority attack with b4-b5 to create a backward pawn on c6 and control the queenside.
common_plans.note: Backward c6 pawn is the stated target.

common_plans.claim: Black neutralises White's queenside pressure while seeking counterplay in the centre or launching a kingside attack.
common_plans.note: ...c5, ...f5, and e-file pushes are the standard counters.

common_plans.claim: Both sides manoeuvre pieces to control key squares (especially c4, c5 and e4) and exploit the fixed pawn structure.
common_plans.note: c4 is a knight outpost for Black, e4 is the break square for White.

common_plans.claim: Both sides transition into an endgame where structural advantages or disadvantages become decisive.
common_plans.note: Wikipedia's minority attack article says the minority attack often yields passed pawns that decide the endgame.
